[scikit-ai](https://github.com/georgedouzas/scikit-ai) provides task-oriented components for text, images, audio and video that
follow the scikit-learn estimator API.

Components are named by what goes in and what comes out, like `ImageClassifier`, `AudioSegmenter` or `TextToVideoGenerator`, so the
name tells you what each one does. Since they are estimators, they fit into `Pipeline`, `GridSearchCV` and the rest of scikit-learn.

Here is a text classifier that learns from a few labelled examples:

```python
from skai.classification import TextClassifier

X = ['I loved this movie.', 'The product broke after a day.', 'Great service!', 'Never again.']
y = ['positive', 'negative', 'positive', 'negative']

classifier = TextClassifier(k_shot=2, random_state=0, backend='dummy').fit(X, y)
print(classifier.predict(['What a wonderful day.']))
```

```
['negative']
```

The `backend` parameter decides what actually runs the task. It can be local open-source models through Hugging Face, the OpenAI API,
other providers through LiteLLM, or models hosted on Replicate. The code stays the same.

I used the `dummy` backend above, which is why it calls a wonderful day negative. It comes with the base install and needs no models
or credentials, but its outputs are placeholders, so swap it for a real one to get real predictions.

Note that `fit` doesn't train a model unless you ask for fine-tuning. A classifier, for example, keeps your samples as examples for
the model to work from.

Install it with `pip install scikit-ai`, and add an extra such as `scikit-ai[hf]` or `scikit-ai[openai]` for the backend you want.
